summary: Extends the Access Node Control Protocol with capabilities for multicast: replication initiated by the network access server, admission control with white, black, and grey lists, bandwidth delegation, and committed bandwidth reporting. It updates RFC 6320.

eli5.summary: When many homes watch the same TV channel, the network should send it only once and decide who is allowed to join. This adds those controls to the protocol that links network equipment.

subtitle: How a broadband network access server and an access node cooperate to replicate, admit and meter multicast video.

tldr.problem: ANCP (RFC 6320) could not support the multicast use cases of the ANCP framework (RFC 5851), so a network access server and an access node had no standard way to share control of multicast replication, admission and bandwidth.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC adds seven new message types, fourteen new TLVs and five negotiable multicast capabilities: NAS-initiated replication, white/black list control, grey list control, bandwidth delegation and committed bandwidth reporting.
tldr.outcome: A NAS and an access node can split multicast duties in several ways, and the capabilities can be combined by rules the RFC gives. It updates RFC 6320 by assigning capability type 3 and changing an IANA result-code boundary.

today: RFC 7256 is a Proposed Standard, and the metadata lists no replacement or later update. It updates RFC 6320, the base ANCP specification, by assigning capability type 3 and changing the IANA result-code boundary from 0x100 to 0x64.

sections.title: What the Multicast Extensions Add
sections.content:
RFC 5851 defines a framework for controlling an Access Node (AN, for example a DSLAM) from a Network Access Server (NAS), and RFC 6320 specifies the Access Node Control Protocol (ANCP) for it. RFC 6320 covers three DSL use cases: topology discovery, line configuration and remote connectivity test. It does not cover the multicast use cases of the framework.

This RFC supplies them, plus one extra use case, committed bandwidth reporting. They are organized into five ANCP capabilities, which can be combined under the rules in the RFC. Because the capabilities share much protocol content, the RFC describes the messages once and then uses tables to say which parts each capability must implement.

The requirements were written with IPTV in mind. Two assumptions underlie them: the Home Gateway is in bridged mode, and multicast signaling uses IGMP (RFC 2236, RFC 3376) or MLD (RFC 3810) rather than PIM. The capabilities do not depend explicitly on the signaling type, but PIM would add implementation complexity.
sections.eli5: There are two boxes in the network, a boss and a helper near the houses. This document teaches them how to share the job of delivering TV channels.

sections.title: The Five Capabilities
sections.content:
In NAS-initiated multicast replication, join and leave requests end at the NAS, or reach it by other means such as application signaling. The NAS tells the AN to start or stop replicating specific flows on specific subscriber ports. The NAS sends one copy of the stream toward the AN, and the AN copies it to subscribers.

In conditional access and admission control with white and black lists, join and leave requests end at the AN. The AN accepts or ignores them according to per-port lists provisioned by the NAS. The grey list variant is similar, except that before accepting a request matching a grey list entry, the AN asks the NAS for permission.

Bandwidth delegation lets the AN and NAS share the total video bandwidth of an access line, for example when the AN does multicast admission control and the NAS or Policy Server does unicast admission control. Committed bandwidth reporting has the AN report how much multicast bandwidth it has granted to a line each time that value changes, optionally buffered so one message covers several lines.

Each capability also supports the multicast accounting and reporting services of RFC 5851. The NAS may also query the AN about which flows are active on which ports (multicast flow reporting).
sections.eli5: Think of a school hallway. Sometimes the principal decides who goes through a door. Sometimes the hall monitor has a list of who may go, and sometimes he asks the principal first about certain kids.

sections.title: The New ANCP Messages
sections.content:
The RFC adds message types 144 to 150. The Multicast Replication Control message (144) is sent by the NAS with one or more Command TLVs, each telling the AN to add (join) or delete (leave) a flow on the target port. Command codes are 1 Add, 2 Delete, 3 Delete All, and 4 to 6 for rejection notices. The AN processes commands in order and stops at the first error. An error from admission control is reported with result code 0x13 "Out of resources".

The Multicast Admission Control message (145) goes the other way: the AN asks the NAS to admit, or notifies it of the removal of, a flow. It can carry the requester's IP address, MAC address or, preferably, a local device identifier. If the NAS accepts an Add, it answers with a Multicast Replication Control message with Result set to Nack (0x1). If it refuses, it MAY send a message carrying one of the reject command codes so the AN can keep statistics.

The Bandwidth Reallocation Request (146) and Bandwidth Transfer (147) messages let either side ask for and hand over delegated bandwidth. Values are totals, not increments, so both sides stay in step. If the NAS has its own request outstanding when the AN's arrives, the NAS rejects the AN's request with result code 0x68 or 0x69. The Delegated Bandwidth Query pair (148) lets either side read the peer's view of the amount.

The Multicast Flow Query pair (149) lets the NAS ask which flows are active on given ports, which ports carry given flows, or everything. The Committed Bandwidth Report (150) is sent by the AN and is never answered. The existing Provisioning and Port Management messages are also reused: Provisioning carries multicast service profiles, and Port Management (function 8) assigns a profile and a bandwidth allocation to a line.
sections.eli5: Each kind of note has its own number: one says "copy this channel here", one says "may I?", and others talk about how much room is left.

sections.title: Multicast TLVs
sections.content:
ANCP messages are built from type-length-value (TLV) pieces. This RFC defines fourteen, among them:

  • Multicast-Service-Profile (0x0013) and Multicast-Service-Profile-Name (0x0018, up to 255 octets): a named bundle of lists. A line is associated with at most one profile.
  • List-Action (0x0021): adds to, deletes from or replaces a white, black or grey list. Entries are prefixes of group and source addresses, so one entry can cover many flows. A prefix length of 0 is a wildcard.
  • Multicast-Flow (0x0019): names a flow as ASM (any source) or SSM (one or more sources), IPv4 or IPv6. Only INCLUDE mode is supported.
  • Bandwidth-Allocation (0x0015) and Bandwidth-Request (0x0016): amounts in kilobits per second as 32-bit values.
  • White-List-CAC (0x0024) and MRepCtl-CAC (0x0025): empty TLVs that tell the AN to do admission control for white-listed flows or for flows added by Multicast Replication Control messages.
  • Report-Buffering-Time (0x0094, milliseconds) and Committed-Bandwidth (0x0095).
  • Request-Source-IP (0x0092), Request-Source-MAC (0x0093) and Request-Source-Device-Id (0x0096), and Sequence-Number (0x0022), which names the failed command in an error reply.
sections.eli5: A TLV is a labeled box: the label says what is inside, how big it is, and then comes the stuff itself. Messages are stacks of these boxes.

sections.title: Capabilities and Procedures
sections.content:
Capabilities are negotiated using the mechanism of RFC 6320, and their Capability Data field is empty. The RFC lists, for each capability, the exact messages and TLVs that MUST be implemented. Receivers MUST ignore content not covered by the negotiated capabilities.

White and black lists. The AN receives the join. It discards requests for black-listed flows and, if admission control is on, discards white-listed ones that would exceed the bandwidth limit. When a flow matches several lists, the most specific match wins: longest group prefix first, then longest source prefix. If equal, black beats white. Flows that match no list SHOULD be discarded unless the white list has a catch-all entry. When a profile changes, the AN reviews active flows and ends any that are now black-listed or unlisted.

Grey lists. A matching join triggers a Multicast Admission Control message to the NAS. If the NAS permits it, it sends a Multicast Replication Control message, and the AN replicates, subject to admission control if enabled. On a leave, the AN stops replicating and tells the NAS.

Combinations. When white, black and grey lists are combined, equal-precision matches are prioritized black, then grey, then white. NAS-initiated replication needs some means to avoid double replication; the simplest is to end all IGMP/MLD at the AN. Committed bandwidth reporting combined only with NAS-initiated replication or grey lists is redundant, since the NAS already knows the same information.

Reporting. The default buffering time is zero, meaning immediate reports. With a non-zero Report-Buffering-Time, the AN starts a timer at the first change, adds or updates one entry per line, and sends the accumulated report when the timer expires.
sections.eli5: The hall monitor checks the guest list from most specific to least, and the "not allowed" list wins any tie.

sections.title: Buffering and Congestion
sections.content:
The RFC gives guidance on choosing a report buffering period. Delay in reporting can cause brief extra demand to be served on a best-effort basis at the NAS, with jitter and packet loss. It cites ITU-T G.1080 for a tolerable loss episode of under 16 ms as an order of magnitude, and works an example suggesting buffering pays off only in larger deployments. Simply switching from one channel to another needs no report or NAS adjustment.

It also warns that a single channel-surfing subscriber can generate enough control messaging to overload the AN or the AN-to-NAS channel. Suggested mitigations include briefly buffering joins in case a matching leave follows (then discarding both), rate limiting per subscriber and globally, and dropping stale requests when overloaded. No quantitative channel zapping delay requirement was available when the RFC was written.
sections.eli5: If one kid keeps flipping channels very fast, the helpers could get swamped with messages, so they wait a moment and skip the ones that are already out of date.

sections.title: Security and Privacy
sections.content:
ANCP security is covered in RFC 6320 and RFC 5713. The RFC says multicast introduces no new security considerations in principle, although it makes ANCP more attractive for denial of service (directing multicast streams onto a target) or theft of service.

The main concern is privacy. Including the requester's IP or MAC address in a Multicast Admission Control message lets an observer track content consumption to a device and perhaps a person. The AN-to-NAS segment is protected by the basic ANCP protection. The NAS-to-AAA path can be protected (Diameter in RFC 6733 mandates IPsec, TLS or DTLS, and RADIUS should use TLS per RFC 6614) or avoided by downloading per-device policy to the NAS. To remove even the NAS as an exposure point, it is RECOMMENDED that the AN map the identifier to a local value known to the AN and AAA only, sent in the Request-Source-Device-Id TLV.
sections.eli5: The messages could reveal which show a particular TV is watching, so the helper uses a secret nickname for each TV instead of its real address.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content:
The RFC registers message types 144 to 150, result codes 0x64 to 0x69 (command error, invalid flow address, multicast flow does not exist, invalid preferred bandwidth amount, inconsistent views of delegated bandwidth amount, bandwidth request conflict), command codes 1 to 6, the TLV types above, and five capability types: 3 for NAS-initiated multicast replication, 5 for committed bandwidth reporting, 6 for white and black lists, 7 for grey lists and 8 for bandwidth delegation. All have technology type 0 and no capability data.

To make room for the new result codes, IANA lowered the starting point for IETF Consensus allocations of result codes from 0x100 to 0x64, which is how the RFC updates RFC 6320.
sections.eli5: New numbers were added to the official list so every maker uses the same number for the same message.

items.label: Multicast Replication Control
items.desc: NAS tells the AN to add or delete flows on a port.

items.label: Multicast Admission Control
items.desc: AN asks the NAS to admit a flow or reports a removal.

items.label: Bandwidth Reallocation Request
items.desc: Either side asks to change the delegated bandwidth.

items.label: Bandwidth Transfer
items.desc: Hands delegated bandwidth to the peer, or answers a request.

items.label: Delegated Bandwidth Query
items.desc: Request and response for the peer's view of the amount.

items.label: Multicast Flow Query
items.desc: NAS asks which flows are active on which ports.

items.label: Committed Bandwidth Report
items.desc: AN reports multicast bandwidth committed to access lines.
